title: Photography direction for an independent school
metaTitle: Photography for an independent school site
excerpt: Photograph students in the day, not the crest. A mission statement in small type is not a substitute for a class a parent can recognize.
alt: Blue and orange ink blooming through water, a diffuse wash with no fixed subject, unlike a school day that needs a recognizable class.
caption: Ink in water is atmosphere. A school photograph needs a class, a task, and a room. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should school photographs show?
faqs.answer: Students and adults who belong to the school, during a real lesson, break, or pickup. The group size and the work should be visible. A shield, an empty stair, and a stock classroom are pictures of an institution, not of a day.

faqs.question: Where does the mission statement belong relative to pictures?
faqs.answer: Not as a caption and not in small type under the hero. If a frame needs the motto to explain it, choose another frame from the same morning. A readable mission can live on the about page after the day has been shown.

faqs.question: What should the alt text include?
faqs.answer: The activity, the rough age, and the setting, without a child's full name and without the motto. People who cannot see the photograph still need to know a class was reading, not that a crest was on the wall. Retire frames when consent changes or the day no longer matches.

markdown:
Independent school website photography has one standard: the picture should show students and the day, not a crest. A mission statement in small type, set under a shield, is the sentence schools use when they do not trust the day to be visible. Reject it as a substitute for the frame. The photographs are part of the argument a parent is having, not a mood pasted beneath a motto.

WCAG treats images as content that still has to be perceivable. A photograph of a class needs a text alternative that says what is happening, including the rough age and the activity, without turning a child into a public profile. Google's people-first guidance makes a related demand: show first-hand experience, and where a "how" matters, show evidence. For a school, the evidence is the day. A crest is not evidence that a child is known.

## The day is the argument

Choose the frame a parent would see if they arrived unannounced on a Tuesday and were allowed to stand quietly at the back. Children working, an adult who belongs there, the room as it is. That frame answers the question the other two schools are also being asked: what happens to my child between the gate and pickup?

Shoot at the height of the room, not from a gallery of architectural pride. Include enough of the group to show its size, and enough of one table to show the work. A close crop of a pencil can be any school. A room with a count is yours.

Put the crest away for these frames. It can sit on a blazer if that is truly how the uniform looks, small, as it looks in life. It should not be the subject. A photograph of a shield on a wall, a motto carved in stone, or an empty staircase with a banner is a picture of the institution admiring itself. Parents cannot leave their child with an emblem.

One stretch of the day, told clearly, beats a montage of every trophy and every lawn. The homepage can carry a single honest frame. Inner pages can carry a sequence: gate, lesson, lunch, pickup. Sequence is an argument. A montage of highlights is a hope that feeling will replace a Tuesday.

## What the day requires in the frame

Light is part of the truth. Photograph the room at the hour the lesson happens, with the lights you actually use. A dim classroom in winter should look like a dim classroom that is still a good place to work, if it is one. Do not wait for a golden hour that never falls during period two. Parents will visit in period two.

Color should match the walls and the uniform. A grade that turns a tired paint job into a magazine blue makes every other claim look slippery. Correct the camera. Stop before you invent a building you do not have.

Scale needs the group. A single child against a blurred background hides whether the class is twelve or twenty-eight. The parent is deciding partly on that number. If the page states a class size, the picture should not obviously contradict it. If the picture was taken on a day when half the class was at a match, say so in the caption, or wait for a full room.

The children must be yours, and the adults must be yours. A library photograph of a diverse classroom that is not your classroom is a false witness. It is also an insult to the children who do attend and were not thought sufficient. If a family has not agreed to public use, do not feature that child as the hero of the frame. Prefer groups, activity, and angles that do not make a face into a poster. This is basic care, and it is also how the picture stays true when a child leaves the school and the page is still up.

Clutter should be school clutter, minus anything that exposes a child's private work to the internet. A staged emptiness, every exercise book hidden, looks like a catalog. Your advantage is a specific room on a specific morning. Do not sand it into a prospectus from a printer's template.

## Why the small mission line is a rejected frame

A mission statement in small type is what gets approved when a photograph of the day felt too ordinary to the committee. The committee wanted the school to sound larger than a Tuesday. The parent needed the Tuesday. Small type is a tell: even the designers did not expect the line to be read. They expected it to bless the crest.

Reject it as the opening, and reject it as the caption under a photograph that does not need a blessing. If the picture shows year 4 reading, the caption can say "Year 4, reading aloud, October." The mission line adds no fact. It adds a fog of excellence that the other schools also purchased.

The same rejection covers a Latin motto in place of a caption, a shield as the hero image, and a film that fades from the crest to a slow lawn before any child appears. Those are the mission statement in other costumes. They spend the first glance on the institution. The parent is in a comparison, and a ceremony does not help them choose.

If the board insists the mission appear, put it on the about page in readable type, under a name, after the day has been shown. Do not set it in 11 pixels under a hero. Illegible type is not a compromise. It is a confession that the sentence cannot earn a place.

Watch the selects beside the mission printout. If a frame needs the motto to explain why it matters, the frame is weak. Choose another frame from the same morning. The motto is not a prosthetic for a picture that failed to show work, care, or group size.

## A shot list for a parent

Direct the photographer with a list that matches the decision, and schedule it during a real day, not a dress rehearsal with borrowed children.

- The gate at the start of school, with the adult who is actually on duty.
- One lesson from the doorway, group size visible, work visible, faces not exploited.
- The same group's table, close enough to see materials, not so close that the room disappears.
- Lunch or break, including the limit of the space if the space is the constraint.
- Pickup, the door you told people to use, the hour it really is.
- One thing you will not glamorize: the stair, the shared yard, the small library.

That is a site. Extra frames are spares. Tell the photographer the lead before the day, so the best attention goes to the lesson and not to the architectural detail over the door.

Ask for a tall crop as well as a wide one. The lead that only works as a banner will lose the children when a phone cuts the sides. Direct the doorway shot so the honest part survives that cut.

## What to refuse

Refuse a lens that makes a yard into a campus. Refuse a composite sky over the building. Refuse posed rows in front of the crest unless that assembly is truly how you gather, and even then do not make it the lead. Refuse children looking at the camera in a line as the main evidence of learning. A look at the camera shows that a photographer was present. A look at the work shows the day.

Refuse a style that needs a haze filter and a soundtrack. Refuse to clear the room of the ordinary mess that proves people were thinking. Refuse any brief that says "more aspirational." Aspirational is the word committees use when they want a different school in the pictures.

Refuse to let the crest open the edit because it is the sharpest file. Sharpness is not relevance. The doorway of the lesson can lead even when the shield is crisper. You are editing an argument about a childhood, not a portfolio for the engraver.

Write the refusals in the same note as the shot list. On the day, someone will want the lawn. A written refusal gives the head and the photographer a rule that does not depend on who is most tired at 3 p.m.

## Captions and alternatives

Write the alt text as a description of the activity and the setting. "A class of junior-age children reading aloud with their teacher, books open, in a room with one window onto the yard." Do not name the child. Do not paste the mission into the alternative. WCAG's point is that someone who does not see the picture still receives the content. The content is the day.

Write a visible caption when the frame needs a year group, a term, or a constraint. "Shared yard, second break, year 3." Captions should not be punchlines or mottoes. If you cannot caption it without the mission line, you do not yet know what the picture is for.

Retire pictures when the children have moved on in a way that makes the frame misleading, or when consent changes. A lead image is not a monument. It is a current claim. Date the set in your own records even if the caption only needs the term.

## The phone will crop the class

Check every select inside a phone-shaped frame before you approve it. A wide lesson that becomes a single blurred ear is no longer evidence. Direction includes the crop. If the group size sits in the part of the frame the phone will cut, recompose while you are still in the room.

That check is the start of the mobile visit, which has its own rules for the first screen and the visit button. [How the first phone screen has to hold the day and the visit](/blog/the-mobile-visit-for-an-independent-school) is the next piece. A correct photograph in a desktop-only layout still loses the parent who never opens a laptop for this decision.

When you want a second opinion on the selects, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). Bring the lesson frame and the crest frame. The conversation is which one leads, and what the caption must say without borrowing the motto.
